newsitem.title: USA: Local TV news devotes most time to crime - survey.
newsitem.headline: Local TV news devotes most time to crime - survey.

text.p: Local television newscasts emphasise crime stories by a wide margin over politics, disasters, health and other types of stories, according to a survey of TV news in eight U.S. cities.

The findings tended to confirm the television adage "if it bleeds it leads" and bolstered the claims of critics that U.S. television newscasts have become a newsreel of stretchers, body bags, yellow police tape and anguished victims.
It was the first known attempt to sample content of local TV newscasts on a national scale, said University of Miami communications professor Joseph Angotti, who headed the survey.

Conducted by the Consortium For Local Television Surveys, the research found that prime-time newscasts in the eight selected cities devoted slightly less than 30 percent of their news time to crime and criminal justice stories, twice as much as the next highest category, government and politics.

Calamities and natural disasters accounted for 10 percent of news time, following by arts and leisure at 8.6 percent, health and medicine at 6.9 percent, education at 2 percent and race relations at 1.2 percent. All other categories accounted for 26.7 percent.
"I think it confirms the worst suspicions that most TV viewers have," Angotti said.

Angotti, a former vice president of NBC News, said the survey sampled local newscasts in Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, Miami, Indianapolis, Austin, Texas, Eugene, Ore., and Syracuse, N.Y. It was conducted on four randomly selected days in November, January, February and April.

Angotti said the heavy emphasis on crime coverage was in large part due to television news consultants who believe that because viewers in urban areas often name crime as their number one concern, it should have the most coverage.
"The consultants tell news directors and producers 'You've got to go out and cover crime.' But that's not really what they (viewers) want," he said. "They want solutions to crime."

He said crime coverage -- which often involves videotape or "live shots" of crime scenes, bodies, blood-stained pavement and wailing relatives -- also is easy to do. "It doesn't take any research. It doesn't take any real skills."
Among the most disturbing aspects of the survey, Angotti said, was the small amount of TV time devoted to coverage of government and virtually non-existent coverage of race relations and education.
"I think one of the reasons they don't cover education is because it's a non-visual story," he said. "There's nothing more boring than a board of education meeting."

Angotti conducted the survey with colleagues at Columbia University, Northwestern University, Syracuse University, University of Southern California, University of Texas, University of Oregon and Ball State University.
In Miami, the station that carried the least amount of crime "by a substantial margin" was ABC affiliate WPLG, the ratings leader at 6 p.m., peak news viewing time, Angotti noted.
"In Miami, at least, crime doesn't pay," he said. "Crime stories do not necessarily translate into higher ratings.
